title: Sets: HashSet, TreeSet, LinkedHashSet
summary: Keep unique values with HashSet, sorted values with TreeSet, and combine sets with union, intersection, and difference.
intro: A set answers one question fast: have I seen this value before? Java gives you three: `HashSet` for fast lookups, `TreeSet` for sorted values and neighbor queries, and `LinkedHashSet` for first-seen order.

steps.title: HashSet basics
steps.body:
A set holds each value at most once. It works like the keys of a map with no values attached. Declare it by the `Set` interface and build a `HashSet`, which, like a `HashMap`, answers `add`, `contains`, and `remove` in about the same short time no matter how big it gets.

```java
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;

Set<String> tags = new HashSet<>();
tags.add("java");               // true: it was new
tags.add("java");               // false: already there, nothing changes
tags.contains("java");          // true
tags.remove("java");            // true: it was there
int n = tags.size();            // 0
Set<Integer> unique = new HashSet<>(list); // duplicates dropped
```

Because `add` returns `false` for a value it already holds, `if (!seen.add(x))` spots a repeat in one call.

A `HashSet` has no order you can rely on. To print one, copy it into a sorted `TreeSet`: `new TreeSet<>(set)`.

For a small fixed set used only for lookups, write `Set.of("a", "b")`. Never print or loop over `Set.of` for output, because its order changes between runs. It is also immutable, and a duplicate inside `Set.of(...)` throws.

Gotcha: unlike `List.remove(int)`, `set.remove(107)` on a `Set<Integer>` removes the value 107, since a set has no indexes.

example.title: Repeated ticket ids
example.prompt: Find the repeated ids in a list, count the unique ids, check them against a fixed VIP set, and remove one.
example.output:
Repeats: [101, 104]
Unique ids: 4
VIP ids: 2
After removing 107: 3, has 107: false
example.explanation: `seen.add(id)` returns `false` the second and third time an id shows up, so those ids go into `repeats`. 104 appears three times but lands in `repeats` once, because a set ignores the extra add. Copying `repeats` into a `TreeSet` prints it sorted. `new HashSet<>(ids)` keeps 101, 104, 107, and 110. Counting VIPs loops over the `HashSet` directly, which is fine because a count does not depend on order. `remove(107)` drops the value, so the size falls to 3 and `contains(107)` is `false`.

practice.title: Repeated fruits
practice.prompt:
Find the repeated fruits in a basket list, then count and check the unique ones.

1. Loop over `fruits` and use the `false` that `add` returns on a `seen` set to collect each repeat into a `repeats` set.
2. Print `Repeats: ` followed by the repeats copied into a `TreeSet`.
3. Build a `HashSet` from `fruits` and print `Unique fruits: ` with its size.
4. Count the unique fruits that are in `tropical` and print `Tropical: ` with the count.
5. Remove `plum` from the unique set, then print `After removing plum: ` with the size, followed by `, has plum: ` and the result of `contains("plum")`.

Expected output:

```text
Repeats: [fig, pear]
Unique fruits: 5
Tropical: 1
After removing plum: 4, has plum: false
```

tests.output:
Repeats: [fig, pear]
Unique fruits: 5
Tropical: 1
After removing plum: 4, has plum: false

hints: Follow the example: `if (!seen.add(fruit))` is true only for a fruit you already saw.
`new TreeSet<>(repeats)` gives a sorted copy to print, and `new HashSet<>(fruits)` drops the duplicates.
Looping over the unique `HashSet` is fine for a count, since the order does not change the total.

steps.title: TreeSet and LinkedHashSet
steps.body:
A `TreeSet` keeps its values sorted, so printing it or looping over it always runs in order. Like a `TreeMap`, it is a little slower than its hash version, so use it when order matters.

To ask about neighbors, declare the variable as `TreeSet<Integer>`, not `Set<Integer>`, because `Set` has no navigation methods.

```java
import java.util.TreeSet;

TreeSet<Integer> t = new TreeSet<>(List.of(30, 10, 20));
t.first();      // 10, the smallest
t.last();       // 30, the largest
t.floor(25);    // 20, largest value <= 25
t.ceiling(20);  // 20, smallest value >= 20
t.higher(20);   // 30, smallest value > 20
t.lower(10);    // null, nothing is < 10
```

These mirror the `TreeMap` methods `firstKey`, `lastKey`, `floorKey`, and `ceilingKey`. `higher` and `lower` are strict: they skip the value itself.

`floor`, `ceiling`, `higher`, and `lower` return `null` when nothing matches. Store the result in an `Integer` and check it with `== null`, because `int x = t.lower(10);` unboxes `null` and throws. On an empty `TreeSet`, `first` and `last` do not return `null`: they throw a `NoSuchElementException`, so check `isEmpty()` first.

A `LinkedHashSet` drops duplicates like a `HashSet` but remembers the order values were first added, which makes it safe to print.

```java
import java.util.LinkedHashSet;

Set<String> order = new LinkedHashSet<>(List.of("b", "a", "b"));
System.out.println(order); // [b, a]
```

example.title: Appointment slots and visited pages
example.prompt: Store appointment minutes in a TreeSet, look up neighbors of a time, then list unique pages in first-seen order.
example.output:
Slots: [540, 600, 690, 780, 900]
Earliest: 540
Latest: 900
Next at or after 620: 690
Last before 620: 600
At or before 600: 600
At or after 901: none
Pages: [home, search, item, cart]
example.explanation: The slots go in out of order, but the `TreeSet` stores them sorted, so it prints from 540 to 900. `first` and `last` read the ends. `ceiling(620)` finds the smallest slot that is at least 620, and `lower(620)` the largest one strictly below it. `floor(600)` includes 600 itself. No slot is at or after 901, so `ceiling` returns `null`, and the ternary prints `none` instead. The `LinkedHashSet` keeps each page the first time it appears and skips the repeats.

practice.title: Bus departures and stops
practice.prompt:
Look up bus departures in a sorted set and list a route's unique stops.

1. Declare `departures` as a `TreeSet<Integer>` and add 375, 330, 420, 495, and 450 in that order.
2. Print `Departures: ` followed by the set.
3. Print `First: ` with the smallest and `Last: ` with the largest departure, each on its own line.
4. Print `Next after 420: ` with the result of `higher(420)`, then `Last before 420: ` with the result of `lower(420)`, each on its own line.
5. Print `At or after 400: ` with the result of `ceiling(400)`, then `At or before 450: ` with the result of `floor(450)`, each on its own line.
6. Store `higher(495)` in an `Integer` and print `Next after 495: ` followed by the value, or `none` when it is `null`.
7. Build a `LinkedHashSet` from `stops` and print `Stops: ` followed by it.

Expected output:

```text
Departures: [330, 375, 420, 450, 495]
First: 330
Last: 495
Next after 420: 450
Last before 420: 375
At or after 400: 420
At or before 450: 450
Next after 495: none
Stops: [Main St, Park, Library, Station]
```

First: 330
Last: 495

hints: Declare `TreeSet<Integer> departures = new TreeSet<>();` so `higher` and `lower` are available.
`higher` and `lower` are strict, so `higher(420)` skips 420 itself. `ceiling` and `floor` include the value you pass.
Print `(next == null ? "none" : next)` inside parentheses so the ternary runs before the concatenation.

steps.title: Set operations
steps.body:
Sets combine with three bulk methods. Each one changes the set you call it on, so copy first when you still need the original.

```java
Set<String> both = new TreeSet<>(a);
both.retainAll(b);    // intersection: keep only what b also has

Set<String> all = new TreeSet<>(a);
all.addAll(b);        // union: add everything from b

Set<String> onlyA = new TreeSet<>(a);
onlyA.removeAll(b);   // difference: drop everything b has

boolean hasAll = a.containsAll(required); // subset test, changes nothing
```

Copying into a `TreeSet` does two jobs at once: the original stays intact, and the result prints sorted. Calling `a.retainAll(b)` directly would quietly shrink `a`, and every later line would see the smaller set.

All four methods take any collection, so `b` or `required` can be a `List`. `addAll`, `retainAll`, and `removeAll` return `true` when the set changed. `containsAll` only reads.

Gotcha: a `TreeSet` of Strings sorts by `compareTo`, so upper case letters come before lower case ones.

example.title: Shared courses
example.prompt: Compute the union, intersection, and difference of two students' course sets as TreeSet copies, and check a required list.
example.output:
Both: [Math, Physics]
Either: [Art, Chemistry, History, Math, Music, Physics]
Only Ana: [Art, History]
Ana unchanged: [Art, History, Math, Physics]
Ana has required: true
Ben has required: false
example.explanation: Each result starts as a fresh `TreeSet` copy of `ana`, so `retainAll`, `addAll`, and `removeAll` change only the copy. That is why `ana` still prints all four courses. `retainAll(ben)` keeps the two shared courses, `addAll(ben)` merges both sets without repeats, and `removeAll(ben)` leaves the courses only Ana takes. `containsAll` checks every course in `required`: Ana has Math and History, Ben is missing History.

practice.title: Movie night
practice.prompt:
Compare two friends' movie sets and check a watchlist.

1. Copy `mia` into a new `TreeSet`, keep only the movies `leo` also watched, and print `Both: ` followed by it.
2. Copy `mia` again, add all of `leo`, and print `All: ` followed by it.
3. Copy `mia` again, remove everything `leo` watched, and print `Only Mia: ` followed by it.
4. Print `Mia still: ` followed by `mia` to show it did not change.
5. Print `Mia saw watchlist: ` followed by whether `mia` contains every movie in `watchlist`.

Expected output:

```text
Both: [Alien, Heat, Up]
All: [Alien, Coco, Heat, Jaws, Rocky, Up]
Only Mia: [Coco, Jaws]
Mia still: [Alien, Coco, Heat, Jaws, Up]
Mia saw watchlist: true
```

tests.output:
Both: [Alien, Heat, Up]
All: [Alien, Coco, Heat, Jaws, Rocky, Up]
Only Mia: [Coco, Jaws]
Mia still: [Alien, Coco, Heat, Jaws, Up]
Mia saw watchlist: true

hints: Start each result with `new TreeSet<>(mia)` so `mia` itself never changes.
Intersection is `retainAll`, union is `addAll`, and difference is `removeAll`.
`mia.containsAll(watchlist)` returns `true` only when every watchlist movie is in `mia`.

recap:
- Declare `Set<E> s = new HashSet<>()` for fast `add`, `contains`, `remove`, and `size`.
- `add` returns `false` for a duplicate, so `if (!seen.add(x))` finds repeats.
- `new HashSet<>(list)` removes duplicates from a list.
- Never print or loop over a `HashSet` or `Set.of` for output. Copy into `new TreeSet<>(set)` first.
- `Set.of(...)` is for small fixed lookup sets: immutable, unordered, and no duplicates allowed.
- `TreeSet` keeps values sorted. Declare `TreeSet<E>` to use `first`, `last`, `floor`, `ceiling`, `higher`, and `lower`.
- `floor`, `ceiling`, `higher`, and `lower` return `null` when nothing matches, so store them in an `Integer` and check for `null`.
- `first` and `last` throw on an empty `TreeSet`.
- `LinkedHashSet` keeps first-seen order.
- Union is `addAll`, intersection is `retainAll`, difference is `removeAll`, and `containsAll` tests a subset.
- The bulk methods change the set they are called on, so copy first to keep the original.
